etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English prejudice, from Old French prejudice, from Latin praeiūdicium (“previous judgment or damage”), from prae- (“before”) + iūdicium (“judgment”).

definitions.definition: (countable) An adverse judgment or opinion formed beforehand or without knowledge of the facts.

quote.citation: 1849–1861, Thomas Babington Macaulay, chapter VII, in The History of England from the Accession of James the Second, volume (please specify |volume=I to V), London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, →OCLC:
quote.text: Though often misled by prejudice and passion, he was emphatically an honest man.

definitions.definition: (countable) A preconception, any preconceived opinion or feeling, whether positive or negative.
(countable) An irrational hostile attitude, fear or hatred towards a particular group, race or religion.
(obsolete) Knowledge formed in advance; foresight, presaging.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book II, Canto IX”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: […]  the first did in the forepart sit, / That nought mote hinder his quicke preiudize: / He had a sharpe foresight, and working wit  […]

definitions.definition: (chiefly obsolete) Mischief; hurt; damage; injury; detriment.

quote.citation: 1793, Benjamin Franklin, The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin‎[1], §20:
quote.text: We both of us happen’d to know, as well as the Stationer, that Riddlesden the Attorney, was a very Knave. He had half ruin’d Miss Read’s Father by drawing him in to be bound for him. By his Letter it appear’d, there was a secret Scheme on foot to the Prejudice of Hamilton, (Suppos’d to be then coming over with us,) and that Keith was concern’d in it with Riddlesden. [...]

quote.citation: 1702, John Locke, translated by W. Popple, A Letter concerning Toleration […] :
quote.text: for no injury is thereby done to any one, no prejudice to another man's goods

quote.citation: 1613 (date written), William Shakespeare, [John Fletcher], “The Famous History of the Life of King Henry the Eight”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
quote.text: England and France might, through their amity, / Breed him some prejudice.

quote.citation: a. 1662 (date written), Thomas Fuller, The History of the Worthies of England, London:  […]  J[ohn] G[rismond,] W[illiam] L[eybourne] and W[illiam] G[odbid], published 1662, →OCLC:
quote.text: For Pens, so usefull for Scholars to note the remarkables they read, with an impression easily deleble without prejudice to the Book.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To have a negative impact on (someone's position, chances etc.).
(transitive) To cause prejudice in; to bias the mind of.
